title: Adherence support for a community falls prevention exercise programme: a pragmatic trial across 14 centres
subtitle: Pragmatic trial with individual allocation in usual classes
statement: Only 38 percent of 520 older adults who started a 24-week community strength and balance programme last year attended at least two thirds of sessions, and few did home exercises. The programme wants to know whether an adherence support package (weekly reminders, two peer volunteer calls and a home exercise calendar reviewed by the instructor) improves attendance and home exercise when delivered in usual classes by usual instructors across 14 centres.
whoAffected: Adults aged 65 and over who have fallen or are at risk of falling, their families, instructors in 14 centres, and trained peer volunteers.
whatHurts: People who stop attending lose the benefit of exercise that prevents falls, and falls lead to injury, fear and loss of independence.
currentPractice: Twice-weekly group classes for 24 weeks with a home exercise sheet; no reminders or follow-up after missed sessions.
whyNow: The programme manager has approved the package and central allocation for the 2027 intakes, and twelve former participants have volunteered as peer supporters.
constraints: No research funding beyond the programme budget. Instructors cannot take on extra data collection; attendance comes from the existing class registers. Peer volunteers are unpaid and trained by the programme. The support package must also work for people without a mobile phone.
patientCenteredGoal: Older adults who join the programme keep exercising long enough to become stronger and steadier and to stay independent at home.
summary: Problem framed as a pragmatic trial of adherence support within the usual programme.
